prompt.context: Your client is Idaho Johnson, an archeologist/adventurer who specializes in rare artifact recovery. They have just learned about the possibility of an incredibly valuable 6,000 year old crown buried in the Siwa Oasis of Northwestern Egypt. You have been hired to determine whether Idaho should launch an expedition to recover this artifact.
prompt.question: Should Idaho Johnson launch an expedition to recover the artifact? Walk through how you would evaluate this investment decision.

clarifying_info.q: How will Idaho finance the dig?
clarifying_info.a: He must self-finance the dig, but he finds a buyer ahead of time and strikes the deal pending the recovery.

clarifying_info.q: How did he learn about the artifact?
clarifying_info.a: A colleague came to him with a map she is willing to sell to him.

clarifying_info.q: Where is the client currently located?
clarifying_info.a: He is currently located in Indiana.

clarifying_info.q: How long will the dig take?
clarifying_info.a: The dig is estimated to take one year (12 months).
He only wants to go on the expedition if he can make an expected ROI of 85%.

clarifying_info.q: What is his estimated chance of success?
clarifying_info.a: He believes he has a 20% chance of successfully retrieving the artifact.

clarifying_info.q: Does he have all the equipment he needs?
clarifying_info.a: He has some equipment but would need to buy more for this expedition.

exhibits.title: Expedition Costs
exhibits.shows: A table listing cost categories and associated amounts for the expedition

framework: Costs: Break into (1) upfront/one-time costs — map, travel, legal, equipment; (2) recurring costs — labor, food/lodging; (3) opportunity costs — teaching salary foregone
Artifact Value: Determine sale structure — one-time payment vs. perpetual revenue share; calculate present value of museum revenue stream
Market Conditions & Buyers: Who will buy? Private collector vs. museum; geography and prestige affect value
Risks: Probability of success (20%); competition finding artifact first; personal danger; self-financing exposure
Alternatives: Other artifacts, safer expeditions, selling the map for profit, film/media franchise

questions.prompt: Question 1: What costs would be required to embark on this expedition?
questions.guidance: Candidate should bucket costs into three categories: (1) Upfront costs — map, travel, legal, equipment; (2) Recurring costs — labor, lodging, food; (3) Opportunity costs — teaching salary, other expeditions foregone.

questions.prompt: Question 2: Calculate the total cost of the expedition using Exhibit 1.
questions.guidance: Candidate must add up all three buckets correctly. Key detail: travel cost is per person and one-way, so must be doubled for round trip. Food/lodging figure is for the entire group, not per person.

math.setup: One-time costs: Map/Equipment + Legal + Travel (round-trip for 6 people including Idaho). Recurring costs: Labor (5 workers x $4K/mo x 12 mo) + Food/Lodging ($10K/mo x 12 mo). Opportunity cost: $100K/yr salary.

questions.prompt: Question 3: There are two buyers — a private collector offering a one-time payment of $4M, and a museum offering a share of exhibit ticket sales. How would you calculate the museum offer's value, and which deal is better?
questions.guidance: Candidate should propose using comparable museum data to project cash flows, then discount to PV using Gordon Growth Model. Strong candidates mention needing to know discount rate and growth rate. Museum deal turns out to be worth $4.5M vs. $4M from collector — museum is the better offer.

math.setup: Museum Attendance = 900,000/yr; % buying exhibit ticket = 50%; ticket price = $10; explorer share = 10%; Discount rate = 15%; Growth rate = 5% (provide discount/growth only if asked).
math.answer: Museum deal PV = $4.5M > $4M private collector. Museum is the better deal.

questions.prompt: Question 4: Given that Idaho has a 20% chance of success, what is the expected ROI? Does it meet his 85% threshold?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate expected revenue as a weighted average of success and failure outcomes, then compute ROI against total costs. Expected ROI comes out to 80%, just below the 85% threshold — this sets up the nuanced recommendation.

math.setup: Success probability = 20%; Failure probability = 80%; Revenue on success = $4.5M (museum deal); Revenue on failure = $0; Total cost = $500K.
math.answer: Expected ROI = 80%, which is below the required 85% threshold.

brainstorming.prompt: Question 1: What costs would be required to embark on this expedition?

recommendation: The expected ROI of 80% is just below Idaho's required 85% threshold, making this a borderline decision. A strong candidate acknowledges both sides and takes a defensible stance — either go or no-go is acceptable with sound reasoning.
risks: ROI (80%) falls short of required ROI (85%)
Probability of success is only 20% — most likely outcome is total loss
Self-financed: Idaho bears full downside risk of the $500K investment
Museum revenue projections rely on comparable data and may be inaccurate
Object could be cursed (humorous but real archeological/reputational risk)
next_steps: If GO: Plan the expedition — assemble crew, gather supplies, book charter plane, finalize museum contract

If NO-GO: Identify other artifact opportunities with better risk-adjusted returns; continue teaching; explore buying and selling the map for profit; pursue synergies (film franchise, book, biography) without the excavation risk
